steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Mate with king and queen: the supported check. This part covers Why it works, and when it fails; Set it up. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Count the squares.** A mate must settle the king's own square (the check) and every neighbour it could step to: up to eight, fewer at an edge. Edward Lasker (*Chess Strategy*, lectures 7 and 8) frames mating as counting squares, with the checking piece safe (checked in our notes). [V] All 364 mating positions of king and queen against a bare king, enumerated here, have the lone king on the edge. [I] In the middle, one queen and one king cannot cover eight neighbours and stay safe.
steps.chapter: Why it works, and when it fails

steps.text: **Three questions for any queen check.** 1. Can the king take her? 2. Is any neighbouring square free? 3. If it is not check at all, does Black still have a legal move? Ask them in this order before every queen move, and the draw traps disappear. Driving the king to the edge is the next skill: see the lesson 'King and queen against king: shrink the box'.

steps.caption: Black to move and checkmated. The five squares around the king are marked. The queen and the white king between them cover all five; f7 and h7 are covered twice.
The same black king, but the white king stands on e6, two files away from the corner squares.

line.say: A check along the back rank, but the king on e6 is too far away to cover g7 or h7.
The king simply steps off the rank. A check is not yet a mate.

steps.caption: Same position again. This check looks more forceful, because the queen goes right beside the king.

line.say: The queen lands beside the king, and nothing protects her.
The king takes the queen. Only two bare kings remain: a draw.

steps.caption: Same position, third try. Quiet king moves also keep the win; one of the neatest is the king step to f6.

line.say: The patient move: the king steps nearer, so that it covers g7 and the squares beside it.
Suppose Black steps into the corner.

Now the queen lands beside the king on a protected square: checkmate. If Black goes to f8 instead, the queen's check on the back rank is mate, because the king on f6 covers e7, f7 and g7. [V: search here] This mates in two; several other quiet moves win more slowly.

steps.text: **Who needs protection?** A king can capture only on a square beside it. So a check from far away needs no protector; it needs every flight square covered. A check from beside the king must be protected, or the king takes the queen. [I] 'Protect the queen' is a good slogan up close and a poor one at long range: ask *can the king take her, and where else can it go?*

steps.caption: A king in the middle has up to eight neighbours, and here five legal replies, so no single check can mate it. Mate happens at the edge, so the king must first be driven there. [V]
Black to move, not in check, with no legal move. This position came from the kings-facing position, one queen move away from mate.

steps.text: **The stalemate trap.** The last queen move can leave the lone king with no legal move and no check: a draw, not a win. [H] It happens when attention jumps from the king's squares to the squares the queen covers, so the 'tighter' move feels better. Ask: does it give check? If so, can the king take her and is any square free? If not, does Black still have a legal move?

**The quiet move.** Often the queen cannot give mate yet, so you first take away the king's last squares. A quiet move works when every reply loses. Count Black's legal moves after yours: when one is left, the mate usually shows. The king helps by covering squares, and by standing ready to protect the queen. [H] Learners may like the close check because it feels nearer the kill; it also needs a protector.

steps.caption: Black's king on d8 has several squares. No check is mate yet.

line.say: A quiet move: the queen covers the whole c-file and checks nothing.
The king goes to e8, its only free square.
The queen checks along the back rank, with the kings facing each other. Checkmate.

steps.caption: Here a king move comes first. Whatever Black replies, a queen check follows on the first rank.

line.say: The king covers a2, b2 and c2, so the black king cannot come up the board.
Black chooses a1. The other choice, c1, also loses to a queen move.
The queen checks along the first rank. The king on b3 covers the second rank. Checkmate.

steps.caption: The king steps in front of the black king and the queen waits on the side. One careless queen move later would be stalemate.

line.say: The king steps up, covering g7 and h7. Only g8 is left for the black king.
The queen checks along the back rank. The king on g6 covers f7, g7 and h7. Checkmate.

steps.caption: Sometimes the first move is itself a check that forces the king to one square.

line.say: A check that covers g8 and g7. Only h7 is left for the king.
The queen lands beside the king, protected by the white king. Checkmate.

steps.text: **Remember.** Before any queen move, ask three things: can the king take her, is a neighbouring square free, and does Black still have a legal move? A check from beside the king needs your king to protect her. If no mate exists yet, play a quiet move that leaves one reply. It fails when Black has no legal move and is not in check: that is stalemate, a draw.
